opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy is actually quite close. When you start as an assistant professor in North America, you're essentially given a small amount of seed funding, a startup package, and some space, and then you're told: go build something. Nobody hands you a team. You have to recruit your first students, and that's very much like hiring your first employees. You're trying to convince talented young people to bet several years of their lives on you, when you don't yet have a track record as a lab, maybe not even a clear brand. So you're selling a vision.

Then there's fundraising. Your startup package runs out, and you have to keep writing grants, building relationships with industry, finding compute. Especially in AI now, compute is like capital. Without it, you can't really compete, so a lot of my energy goes into figuring out how to get resources so the students can do ambitious work.

And there's the question of product, or in our case, research direction. A startup has to find product-market fit; a lab has to find its research taste and identity. What problems are we going to be known for? What do we believe that other people don't yet believe? If you just follow whatever is hot, you're competing with huge industry labs with far more resources, and you'll lose. So, like a startup, you need to find a niche, a contrarian bet, something where a small, focused team can actually make a difference.

Finally, there's culture. In the early days, the PI is basically the founder: you set the tone for how people collaborate, how open you are, how much risk you tolerate, how you deal with failure. Those early decisions compound. The first few students shape the lab almost as much as I do.

The big difference, of course, is that the "output" isn't revenue, it's people and ideas. Your real product is the students you train. If they go on to do great things, that's the exit, in a sense. But the day-to-day experience of building something from zero, under uncertainty, with limited resources, feels very entrepreneurial.

r001.rationale: The response mentions limited resources and startup funding running out, but does not identify stagnant research funding alongside rising costs as the cause of a widening gap.

r002.rationale: It mentions building industry relationships, but does not say companies reduced academic research funding after ChatGPT or the arrival of the LLM era.

r003.rationale: It says the startup package runs out and the PI must seek grants, industry relationships, and compute to support ambitious work, linking resource constraints to raising support from multiple sources.

fable-5.1.text:
It's an analogy I use a lot, and I think it's more literal than people expect. When you join a university as an assistant professor, you basically get a startup package. That's what it's actually called: a startup package. It's seed funding. The university gives you some money, some space, maybe a couple of years of student support, and then says, go build something. After that, you're on your own.

So from day one you're doing all the things a founder does. You have to raise money, which means writing grants to the NSF, to DARPA, to industry partners, pitching your research vision to people who have a hundred other proposals on their desk. You have to recruit, and recruiting PhD students is very much like recruiting early employees, because the best students have offers from Stanford, from Berkeley, from industry labs paying very well, and you have to convince them that your "company" is where they should spend five or six years of their life. You have to build a culture. You have to figure out what the group is about, what problems we care about, how we work together.

And there's a product too. For us the product is ideas, papers, open-source code, models. If you look at something like ConvNeXt or DiT, those are in some sense products that came out of a small team, and their impact depends on whether the community adopts them. There's a very real market dynamic there. If nobody uses your work, it doesn't matter how elegant it was.

The part that resembles a startup most, I think, is the uncertainty and the autonomy. Nobody tells you what to do. You could spend three years on a direction and it goes nowhere. You have to make bets with limited resources, especially now, when compute is so expensive and a university lab has maybe a few hundred GPUs while the big labs have hundreds of thousands. So you have to be strategic about where a small team can still win. That's exactly the question a startup founder asks: where is the big incumbent not looking, where can we move faster, where does being small actually help?

The difference, of course, is the objective. A startup optimizes for valuation or revenue. We optimize for something fuzzier: knowledge, training people, pushing the field somewhere it wouldn't otherwise go. And our "employees" are supposed to leave. The whole point is that students graduate and go do their own thing. So it's a company whose success is measured partly by how many people walk out the door and build great things elsewhere. That's a strange kind of company, but I find it a really meaningful one to run.

r001.rationale: The response mentions expensive compute and limited lab resources, but does not identify stagnant research funding widening a gap with rising costs.

r002.rationale: It mentions industry partners as a funding source, but says nothing about companies retrenching after ChatGPT or the LLM era.

r003.rationale: It connects the startup analogy to raising money and making bets with limited resources, and names grants to NSF, DARPA, and industry partners as multiple support sources.

astra-6.text:
I think the similarity is that you’re building an organization from scratch. You may start with a research idea, but an idea alone isn’t enough. You have to recruit people, find funding, establish a culture, and decide which problems are worth pursuing. And these things are connected: your research direction attracts certain people, and the people who join will also reshape that direction.

As a professor, you’re not just doing research yourself anymore. You’re responsible for creating an environment where other people can do good research and grow. That requires a different set of skills. How do you communicate a vision while giving students enough freedom to develop their own ideas? How do you balance ambitious, uncertain projects with the resources you actually have? Those feel very much like questions a startup founder faces.

Of course, the goal is different. An academic group isn’t ultimately trying to sell a product. We’re trying to produce knowledge and train researchers. But the process of building the team and sustaining it has a lot in common with starting a company.

r001.rationale: The response mentions balancing projects against available resources, but does not identify stagnant funding, rising costs, or the resulting widening gap.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about corporate funding opportunities or companies pulling back after ChatGPT and the LLM era.

r003.rationale: It compares group-building to founding a startup through recruiting, funding, culture, and direction, but does not explain that resource constraints require faculty to raise support from multiple sources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the similarity is that you’re building an organization from scratch. You need to recruit people, find resources, decide what you’re going to work on, and create an environment where people can do their best work. Having a good research idea is only one part of that.

There’s also a lot of uncertainty. When you start a lab, you don’t know which projects will succeed, whether you’ll get the funding you need, or how the team will develop. You have to set a direction while leaving enough room for people to explore and surprise you.

Of course, the goal is different from a company’s. In an academic group, we’re trying to produce knowledge and train researchers. But the organizational challenge is quite similar: how do you bring talented people together around something meaningful, and help them accomplish things they couldn’t do individually?
